sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
sources.text: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ D escribed as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. From the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia to the painstaking world-building of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictional take on Florida, players have shared their wide-ranging experiences with the Guardian, revealing what has surprised and challenged them about this long-awaited release – and what this all means for the series’ evolution. Pete Langhelt, 39, from Colchester, pre-ordered GTA VI “as soon as I could”, and has been looking forward to its release for a long time. “Out of my group of friends I’m probably the only one really nerding out about it,” he says. While Pete hasn’t been able to take time from work in the civil service, he’s still clocked “about 10 hours” of gameplay already. “The core of the missions themselves are pretty similar,” he says. “You turn up somewhere, shoot a load of people and escape. But the development of the characters has changed an awful lot. I have enjoyed the dynamic between Jason and Lucia. I never thought you could make comfortable domesticity into an enjoyable side activity in a video game.” Pete has played all the installments of GTA franchise from the first, when he was “probably too young to be playing”. “I think Red Dead Redemption 2 was my favourite Rockstar game going into this, and it seems to have developed the things that I really liked about Red Dead.” The game encourages exploration, he says. “The day and night cycle seems a lot less intense than GTA V, meaning you don’t feel rushed to get things done. I can let Jason take a slow start to the day before taking a slow drive or boat ride to whatever criminal activity needs completing.” His partner is less keen. “She’ll have to put up with me being on the Xbox for the next few weeks,” he says. A 59-year-old MBA retiree from Venice, Florida, was also struck by just how much of the experience revolves around everyday life. He described it as the “most beautiful, real, open-world game that’s ever existed”. “I was surprised that, with about 10-plus hours of play, most of my time has been spent performing mundane tasks like home repair, grocery shopping, personal grooming and trying to open a bank account. The realism is incredible, but perhaps too real,” he said. “It’s as fully realized as a game world could be. I never expected to see anything more fully developed,” he added. Rob Smeraldo, 28, from Dundee, took the day off work yesterday to play the game on his PlayStation 5. “I made sure I had loads of snacks and Domino’s,” he says. And already, Rob believes that “GTA VI must be the greatest game ever made”. “I think the realism and just the detail put into it is absolutely astounding. The shadows, the way the hair moves when people move around … They took their time, but it’s definitely been worth it,” he says. Rob is a longtime GTA fan and wore a GTA VI T-shirt and drank from a GTA mug to mark the occasion. “I purchased the physical copy [of the game] as soon as it became purchasable – I just wanted the memorabilia, you know?” Ella Delancey, 35, of Berkshire has been playing GTA since she was a child. “GTA III is a huge core memory for me. My brother and I were much too young to be playing it and I definitely wouldn’t let my daughter play it now, but at the time we were obsessed.” So far, the social and brand director has been surprised by how much there is to do aside from pushing the story forward. “I’m not very far into it yet, but I’m already struck by the graphics and the sheer depth of what you can do. It’s very violent, obviously, but I play by the rules, which probably makes me a bit boring. I’ve been birdwatching and exploring, and there’s so much to do outside the main story.” There is one thing she is struggling with, however, and that’s Lucia, one of the main protagonists, leaving her child in a cafe and going to prison, only to come out and start committing more crimes. “As a mother, that doesn’t sit comfortably with me. I know it’s a game and you have to suspend your morals to a degree, but that part has given me pause,” she says. “I do think it’s a step forward that you can no longer hire sex workers as in previous games. GTA still has a complicated relationship with misogyny – and it’s far from perfect, but that change feels significant.” While Ella hasn’t taken any time off work to play, she has set aside time on Friday to play or watch her partner play. “It’s so immersive that it doesn’t feel like a chore, and I can see it replacing our usual after-work TV downtime for a little while,” she says. Clint, 36, who works in the music industry in Chicago, describes the game as “truly one of one”, pointing to its unexpectedly domestic moments and the relationship between Jason and Lucia as some of its biggest draws. “The story is just downright cute. I just had my character build an Ikea table with his girlfriend, and loved it. I typically skip some cutscenes, but now I’m rewatching them when I miss something,” he says. Clint says Jason and Lucia’s relationship is particularly significant, describing it as an example of healthy masculinity that could resonate with younger players. “The main character’s relationship is healthy (at least so far, at six hours in – and ‘healthy’ for a GTA game), which I see as such a posit

sources.title: ¿Qué ha perdido ‘GTA 6’ comparado con los Grand Theft Auto anteriores?
sources.text: El hype por GTA 6 ha pagado con creces. Lo nuevo de Rockstar Games debutó en los últimos días con una respuesta inmejorable tanto del público como de la crítica especializada. La espera de 13 años para tener un nuevo Grand Theft Auto ha valido la pena, aunque a los jugadores también les ha llamado la atención la ausencia de algunas características de sus predecesores . Algunas de estas omisiones tienen una explicación totalmente narrativa, mientras que otras responden a una decisión práctica por parte de los desarrolladores. Está claro que GTA 6 es una propuesta con cada detalle cuidado al extremo y que apunta a brindar la experiencia más inmersiva (y realista) en la historia de la saga. Esto también implica que han tenido que enfocarse en la imagen grande y hacer algunas concesiones en beneficio de la historia que plantea GTA 6 . El caso más notorio es que ya no puedes contratar prostitutas , algo que ya formaba parte del ADN de la franquicia. Pero ojo, que esto no responde a que en Rockstar se hayan vuelto mojigatos o les carcoma la conciencia . Desde la compañía explicaron a ShackNews que quitaron dicha función para resaltar el componente crucial del juego, que es la evolución del vínculo entre Jason y Lucía. “ GTA VI es un juego sobre una pareja en una situación complicada: amantes a la fuga. Si bien hemos conservado muchos elementos de entregas anteriores de GTA , todo lo que hemos implementado en esta sexta entrega responde al espíritu de la historia que queríamos contar y a los sistemas de juego que deseábamos ampliar, tales como el sistema de búsqueda policial, la radio, los atracos y el robo de vehículos. Aunque muchos aspectos de títulos anteriores no están presentes en GTA VI , consideramos que los elementos que hemos incluido son necesarios y complementarios para transmitir las sensaciones y motivaciones que queríamos destacar a lo largo de la historia de Jason y Lucía”. Esto no quiere decir que los jugadores estén obligados a cultivar la relación romántica entre Jason y Lucía. GTA 6 les da la libertad a los jugadores de decidir si quieren que los protagonistas sigan juntos o si prefieren que rompan . No obstante, el hilo conductor que se presenta desde el comienzo incluye un objetivo en común que excede a los protagonistas. Así, incluir la opción de contratar prostitutas parece algo innecesario y descartable . Es cierto que las primeras horas de GTA 6 tienen un poco de girlfriend simulator , pero también es una realidad que transitar ese camino paga con creces cuando las cosas dan un giro para lo peor. Sin meternos en spoilers, hay un punto de quiebre en la misión para trabajar con Mattia que pone todo en su lugar. Pero mucho antes de llegar a esa parte, ni recordarás que el juego no te permite contratar prostitutas y matarlas para recuperar tu dinero. GTA 6 está plagado de minijuegos y actividades complementarias. Sin embargo, los jugadores han notado que falta uno que ya era un clásico de la saga Grand Theft Auto y de GTA Online . Nos referimos, claro, a los dardos . Pero no es el único ausente, pues lo nuevo de Rockstar Games tampoco permite jugar a los bolos . Rockstar también ha dado una explicación sobre esto. La firma prefirió dejar de lado algunos minijuegos en GTA 6 porque ya no había tiempo para hacerlos como correspondía . Estas actividades sirven como una extensión de las físicas del juego, algo que se puede ver en las partidas de pool en The Rusty Anchor, y desarrollarlas como correspondía habría demandado una carga todavía mayor sobre el equipo. Después de todo, cada minijuego es un videojuego con vida propia dentro de otro videojuego. “El caso de los dardos es polémico. A veces se oye decir que hay dinero o tiempo ilimitados, pero ni siquiera nosotros disponemos de ello. Por eso, a veces hay que reconocer que no vamos a ser capaces de alcanzar el nivel que consideramos necesario”, explicó Rob Nelson, uno de los jefes de Rockstar North, a VGC .

stories.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
stories.summary: Trump said he discussed Jensen Huang with China's Xi. Bessent said the ousted Nvidia CEO didn't come up in talks he had while in China.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
sources.text: President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference. Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating. A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations. Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO. "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies." Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week. The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries. Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week. "We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said. "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China. The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors. Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO. Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race. Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI. They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI. In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed. Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview. On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped. Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions." "I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors. Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show. Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.

stories.title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
stories.summary: What can AI enable in medicine, and how do we get there? Microsoft Research lead Doug Burger, Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini, Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz, and physician-scientist Eric Topol of Scripps Research explore these questions and more. The post Can AI help build a healthier future? appeared first on Microsoft Research .

sources.name: Microsoft Research
sources.title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
sources.text: By Doug Burger , Technical Fellow and Corporate Vice President, Microsoft Research Ava Amini , Principal Research Manager Eric Horvitz , Chief Scientific Officer Dr. Eric Topol , Executive Vice President, Scripps Research Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first? Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential. This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come. DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse. Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come. In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI. Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend. Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab) , the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab) . So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician. Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo , a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer. So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here. It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable. And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI. I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava. I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare. Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists. In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcar

recent_posts.title: Petição pela volta de Huang à Nvidia passa de 170 mil assinaturas
recent_posts.summary: Elon Musk e outros executivos de tecnologia apoiaram publicamente o pedido de recondução do ex-CEO, segundo a TechCrunch e a CNBC.

recent_posts.title: Roboflow lança reconhecimento de ações em vídeo na sua IA
recent_posts.summary: Plataforma de visão computacional passa a identificar sequências de ações em vídeo, com início e fim de cada etapa, segundo a empresa.

recent_posts.title: Microsoft acha brecha que instala backdoor em agentes de IA
recent_posts.summary: Pesquisadores da empresa alteraram menos de 10 neurônios de um modelo sem retreiná-lo e fizeram um agente de IA executar código malicioso ao detectar um gatilho oculto.

recent_posts.title: Hugging Face reduz espaço de busca por IA sem perder precisão
recent_posts.summary: Nova técnica de treinamento, batizada de pooling-aware training, comprime até quatro vezes as representações usadas em busca com inteligência artificial e mantém quase toda a precisão, segundo a empresa.

recent_posts.title: Amazon lança Mitra-v2, modelo aberto para dados em tabelas
recent_posts.summary: Segunda versão do modelo de fundação para tabelas tem pesos abertos no Hugging Face e já é usada internamente pela empresa.
